spots.label: Electrical panel
spots.what: Every circuit in the house starts here, behind its own breaker. Old panels, full ones and loose connections are where many electrical problems begin.
signs: A breaker that trips again and again
Warm spots, a buzzing sound or a burning smell at the panel
No room left for a new circuit

spots.label: Meter & service
spots.what: Power comes from the pole, down the mast and through the meter. The parts up to the meter usually belong to the utility; the rest of the run is yours.
signs: Lights dim all over the house when something big starts
A damaged mast, loose wires or a cracked meter box
Half the house out while the rest still works

spots.label: Kitchen outlets
spots.what: Kitchens, bathrooms, garages and outdoor spots need GFCI protection, which cuts the power in a split second when current goes where it shouldn't.
signs: An outlet that's warm, loose or scorched
A GFCI outlet that won't reset, or never trips when tested
Plugs that fall out of the socket

spots.label: Lights & switches
spots.what: A light that flickers is often just a bulb, but a loose connection in a box or switch heats up every time it carries power.
signs: Flickering that a new bulb doesn't fix
A switch or dimmer that feels warm
Bulbs in one fixture burning out fast

spots.label: EV charger
spots.what: A home charger pulls a lot of power for hours. It needs its own circuit, sized for it, and a panel with room to spare.
signs: The breaker trips while the car charges
A plug or charger that gets hot

spots.label: Smoke alarms
spots.what: Wired-in smoke alarms are linked, so when one sounds they all do. They only work if they're powered and not too old.
signs: A chirp every minute or so
One alarm sounds and the others stay quiet

title: What's happening
with your power?
helper.intro: Pick the closest one. Here's what to do in the next five minutes, and when to stop and call.

items.label: A breaker tripped
steps: Unplug or switch off what was running on that circuit when it went out.
At the panel, push the tripped breaker firmly to Off, then back to On.
If it trips again straight away, leave it off. That circuit has a fault we need to find.
items.note: Never tape or hold a breaker on. It trips to stop wires from overheating.

items.label: Outlets are dead
steps: Look for a GFCI outlet nearby, the kind with Test and Reset buttons, and press Reset. One GFCI can protect several outlets.
Check the panel for a tripped breaker.
Still dead? Don't open the outlet. Call us.
items.note: GFCI outlets are often in the kitchen, bathrooms, garage or outside, sometimes in a different room from the dead outlet.

items.label: Lights flickering
steps: One light: switch it off, let it cool, and check the bulb is screwed in firmly. Try a new bulb.
Lights dim when the AC or the microwave starts? Note which ones. It helps us find the circuit.
Flickering all over the house: call us, and your utility if the neighbors have it too.
items.note: A flicker with a buzzing or crackling sound means turn it off at the switch and call us.

items.label: Burning smell or sparks
steps: If it's safe to reach, turn off the breaker for that room, or the main breaker.
Don't touch the outlet, switch or anything plugged into it.
Smoke or flames: get everyone out and call 911.
items.note: A downed power line outside? Stay well away, keep others back, and call 911 and your utility.

title: What are your bulbs
really costing?
led_calc.intro: Slide to the old bulbs still in your house, how long they're on, and your rate.
led_calc.hint: Your rate is on your electric bill, in cents per kWh.
led_calc.source: A rough estimate: bulbs × watts × hours a day × 365 ÷ 1,000 × your rate. It compares 60-watt incandescent bulbs with 9-watt LEDs that give about the same light (800 lumens). The Department of Energy says LEDs use at least 75% less energy and last up to 25 times longer than incandescent bulbs.

faq.q: Why does my breaker keep tripping?
faq.a: Usually too much on one circuit, a short, or a ground fault. Unplug what's on it and reset it once. If it trips again, leave it off and call us.

faq.q: Can my panel handle an EV charger?
faq.a: Often, but not always. We look at your panel and how much power the house already uses before we put anything in, and tell you straight if it needs an upgrade.
An outlet that cuts the power in a split second if current leaks where it shouldn't, like through water or a person. Kitchens, bathrooms, garages and outdoor outlets should have them.

faq.q: How often should smoke alarms be replaced?
faq.a: Test them every month, and replace them at least every 10 years, which is what the National Fire Protection Association recommends.

faq.q: Do you tell me the price before you start?
faq.a: Yes. Once we've seen the problem we tell you what it will cost, and the work only starts when you agree.
Many electrical jobs, like panels, new circuits and EV chargers, need a permit and an inspection in most towns. We'll tell you what yours asks for.
